Photograph: Olivia Bowden Canada Canadian airline WestJet agrees to settle flight attendants’ sexual harassment class action Female staff alleged company failed to maintain safe workplace, after allegations of sexual assault against pilot Olivia Bowden in Toronto Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.40 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 12.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Canadian airline WestJet has agreed to pay C$4.5m (£2.4m) to settle a decade-long sexual harassment class action lawsuit levelled by its female flight attendants, who alleged the company failed to maintain a safe workplace. The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis, a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague, but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk. A British Columbia judge on Monday approved the terms of the settlement, which were finalised on 22 June after months of negotiation. The payment will be distributed among the 3,452 flight attendants in the class action after expenses are removed, including legal fees. WestJet agreed to hire a third-party to conduct a workplace inquiry that will examine the prevalence of harassment, the extent of underreporting and how reporting systems can be made more effective. The suit had called on WestJet to implement mandatory anti-harassment training for pilots, along with an admission of wrongdoing and an admission of a breach of employee contract. None were included in the settlement. Lewis filed the initial class action against the airline in April 2016. She said she was dismayed by the results, especially given that two years ago WestJet paid out $12.5m in a baggage fee class action, nearly three times the amount agreed to in the sexual harassment suit. “I’m glad it’s over … but I’m just exhausted. I’m shaking my head,” she said, adding that she was advised the amount was the most that could be achieved given that legal expenses were piling up. Under BC law, the suit included all female flight attendants who worked for the company between 4 April 2014 and 28 February 2021, because Lewis’s suit alleged that all of them had their contracts violated by WestJet during that period because its employee policy promised that the workplace would be free from harassment. The suit claimed WestJet broke its policy by not taking enough steps to address reports of assault or to prevent harassment in the first place. Lewis said she was sexually assaulted by a WestJet pilot while on a layover in Hawaii in 2010 when she was 25 years old. In court documents, she said the same pilot had also assaulted another flight attendant in 2008. Though she reported the assault to WestJet, the pilot remained at the company and Lewis was eventually fired in 2016 for “gross insubordination”, according to court documents submitted by WestJet that year, which she and her legal team allege was retaliation for trying to hold the airline accountable internally. She said she abandoned an individual civil claim and instead created the class action after learning other flight attendants had also experienced harassment. Lewis said she reported the assault to police in Maui but alleges WestJet rerouted the pilot so he would not face questioning in Hawaii. She said fellow members of the class action suit were also disappointed with the result. Eight of them had already asked the province’s supreme court not to approve the settlement in February when some of the details first emerged, citing a low payout and a lack of accountability by WestJet. “We didn’t get justice here,” said Lewis. The case garnered national attention for exposing pilot behaviour toward female flight attendants and the vulnerability of the scores of young women who have historically been the target demographic for the job. A 2018 survey of more than 3,500 flight attendants by the US Association of Flight Attendants found that 68% had experienced sexual harassment in their careers while only 7% had reported an incident to their employer. WestJet did not respond to questions about Lewis’s claims of assault, and the allegations that it failed to keep the workplace free of harassment and does not properly investigate alleged sexual assaults. In a statement, the company said it was “pleased to have reached a mutually agreed upon settlement”. It said: “We are committed to strengthening our operations and training, focused on the safety and wellbeing of all WestJetters and we are focused on advancing a culture of empowerment.” Explore more on these topics Canada Sexual harassment Air transport Airline industry Americas news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4557.text: This year's spring census confirmed that the population of the Tatra chamois (a goat-like antelope, kamzik in Slovak) is developing favourably, the Tatra National Park (TANAP) Administration reported, adding that experts from the Slovak and Polish sides of the High Tatra mountains counted a total of 786 chamois, which is 46 more than last year. "Even more encouraging is the news of new life in the Tatra mountains: as many as 95 young have been born this year, confirming that the chamois population is in good health and breeding successfully. These results are down to the dedicated work of experts, staff at TANAP Administration, the Polish Tatra National Park, volunteers and everyone who helps to protect this precious symbol of the Tatra Mountains," said conservationists. The joint Slovak-Polish chamois census has been carried out continuously since 1959 and is one of the oldest wildlife monitoring programmes in Europe. This year, it was divided into several stages, during which individuals were counted in various locations in the Western, High and Belianske Tatra mountains. The Tatra chamois is endemic to the region, and the aim of the spring census was to determine population growth following the winter. Source: TASR

Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images US economy Analysis ‘Starve the beast’? The $40tn cost of Republicans’ false promises to cut spending Eduardo Porter The enormous US debt under Trump will hobble the next Democratic administration – just as the GOP planned Why is the Trump administration causing turmoil in the bond markets? Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.21 EDT Last modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.40 EDT Share You could pin the US’s staggering $40tn in government debt to Donald Trump’s Keystone Cops-style governance. Tariffs he sold as a new source of revenue were struck down by the supreme court, forcing the government to return tens of billions of dollars to importers. Elon Musk’s “department of government efficiency” (Doge), ostensibly created to stop wasteful government spending, decimated federal programs and probably killed millions of children , but did nothing to close the budget deficit. The burst of inflation following Trump’s misguided adventure in Iran sharply raised the cost of serving the government’s obligations. Yet as the federal debt hits an all-time high, up from about $35tn when Trump took office less than two years ago, it is worth noting that the US’s gargantuan indebtedness is in fact the product of a longstanding Republican strategy that took shape well before Trump could even dream about gold-plating the White House. It was called “starve the beast”. One might recall Ronald Reagan’s address to the nation on 5 February 1981, just two weeks after he had taken office, when he delivered the sad news that “we’re in the worst economic mess since the Great Depression”. Government spending was out of control, he said. The budget deficit the year before had hit 2.6% of the nation’s gross domestic product. Federal debt added up to a mind-boggling trillion dollars, a third of gross domestic product (GDP) – the broadest measure of the national economy. US gross national debt tops $40tn for first time Read more To end the government’s profligacy, Reagan argued, required depriving it of revenue. “There were always those who told us that taxes couldn’t be cut until spending was reduced,” Reagan said. “Well, you know, we can lecture our children about extravagance until we run out of voice and breath. Or we can cure their extravagance by simply reducing their allowance.” And starving the government beast of tax revenue became the goal of Republican economic policy. The staggering budget deficit left behind by Reagan forced his successor, George H. W. Bush, to raise taxes, which cost him re-election. Every Republican administration since that speech has taken a machete to the tax schedule, slashing income tax rates for businesses and individuals, cutting estate taxes, and carving out broad tax deductions for preferred constituencies. What remained unsaid, over nearly half a century worth of tax cuts, was that the ultimate goal of the plan was not really to cure the “extravagance” and fix the government’s finances. It was, instead, to cement the Republicans’ hold on power. Why is US bond market turmoil hitting governments worldwide? | Richard Partington Read more Despite Republicans’ sloganeering, their tax cuts never “paid for themselves” by generating a burst of economic growth. Instead, they borrowed the money to keep up spending. That invariably left Democrats in a budgetary mess to clean up every time they came into office. Bruce Bartlett, a former Republican policy adviser who worked on a precursor to Reagan’s 1981 tax cut plan, explained the strategy thus: “It’s all part of Republican plan going on for quite a long time to tie the hands of Democratic presidents.” The huge tax cuts in Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) will “make sure the next Democratic president is a complete and total failure”. History may come to see Trump’s “beautiful bill” as an unprecedented attack on the nation’s public finances. The federal deficit (the annual shortfall when the government spends more money than it takes in) is now running at about 6% of GDP. The federal debt (the total owed) is running at about 123% of GDP, higher than during its peak in the second world war. Last year, paying interest on that debt cost 3.2% of GDP, about a trillion dollars, more than was spent on national defense or Medicare. Republicans have never been punished politically for their dismal stewardship of the budget Destructive though it appears, the OBBBA was just one big step along a path set 45 years ago. Federal government revenues declined as a share of GDP in every Republican administration since Reagan’s. Budget deficits widened every time. The precedent bodes ill for the Democratic administration that seems likely to succeed Trump’s unhinged four years in power. Bill Clinton’s administration offers the starkest example. Boxed in by a budget deficit equal to 4.5% of GDP that he inherited from George HW Bush, Clinton was forced to focus on deficit reduction . “Clinton comes with all these plans and ideas but they all get stomped on,” Bartlett recalled. Rather than shore up the US’s threadbare safety net, Clinton ended “ welfare as we know it ”, putting a stop to Democrats’ longstanding commitment to poverty alleviation. He raised taxes, despite their unpopularity, raising federal revenues over his eight years in the White House from 17% to 20% of GDP. At the end of his term, he bequeathed a budget surplus of 2.3% of GDP. His successor, George W Bush, happily spent the inheritance on huge tax cuts that largely benefited the rich. To be fair, the OBBBA, the latest chapter in the Republican’s fiscal path of destruction, did cut spending – $1tn-plus from Medicaid and food assistance programs for the poor. But that was no match for $5tn-plus worth of tax cuts doled out largely to the most affluent Americans . And this leaves Democrats , again, in a budgetary pickle. If the optimistic predictions come to pass and they win control of both houses of Congress in November and the presidency in 2028, they will arrive into the seat of power with at least one hand tied behind their back. Ambitious, expensive ideas like Medicare for All or allowances for families with children will struggle, given the ballooning deficits and debt Trump left in their way. Even undoing Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, food stamps and subsidies for health insurance under Obamacare will seem forbidding. Republicans have never been punished politically for their dismal stewardship of the budget. Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden didn’t gain much from efforts towards deficit reduction. But it won’t be easy for Democrats to simply take a page from the GOP’s playbook. Financial markets are jittery. Rising bond yields alone will raise the government’s cost of servicing the debt, crowding out Democratic spending priorities. That’s hardly the end of it. Once Democrats are in the White House, Republicans will surely rediscover their long-lost concerns about the government’s lack of fiscal restraint, and do their standard budget hawk cosplay thing to force Democrats to fix the budget. Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. https://praguemonitor.com/work-life/how-.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points Czechia has three network operators, O2, T-Mobile and Vodafone, plus virtual operators that rent capacity on those networks. Prepaid needs little paperwork; a contract needs identity documents and often a Czech address, and a first commitment for consumers is limited by law to 24 months. You can keep your number when you switch operator, and the Czech Telecommunication Office handles unresolved complaints. On this page 8 sections The networks Prepaid, contract or a virtual operator What to compare Getting a number: a short guide Keeping your number A hypothetical first month Shops, apps and the small print Invoices, fees and problems The first thing most newcomers do after landing is something with a phone. A Czech number opens the door to banking apps, delivery drivers, landlords and the text-message codes that state services use. It is also the first contract many newcomers sign here, which makes it a useful lesson in reading what happens after the introductory price ends. There are three ways to get a number: a prepaid SIM, a contract with an operator and a plan from a virtual operator. Which is right depends on how long you will stay, what documents you hold and how much data you really use. The networks Czechia has three nationwide mobile network operators: O2, T-Mobile and Vodafone (brand names as of 2026). Each runs its own network and sells under its own name. Around them sits a group of virtual operators, which buy capacity from one of the three and sell their own plans, often with simpler pricing and no store network. The difference to you is mostly in price, customer service and coverage in your particular street or village. All three networks offer 4G and 5G in towns, and coverage thins out in some rural areas and in some buildings. Because coverage is local, the sensible test is to ask friends or neighbours which network works inside your building. Operators publish coverage maps, and a map is a start but not a guarantee indoors. The regulator is the Czech Telecommunication Office ( Český telekomunikační úřad , ČTÚ). It supervises the market, publishes information for consumers and settles certain disputes. Prepaid, contract or a virtual operator Choosing between the main routes Feature Prepaid SIM Contract with an operator Virtual operator plan Paperwork Little; often ID at purchase Identity document, Czech address, sometimes proof of income Often online with ID Commitment None Fixed term, up to 24 months for consumers Often none or short Cost pattern Top up as you go Monthly fee, device instalments possible Monthly fee, often simpler Best for Arrival, short stays, tourists Long stays, a new phone on instalments Price-conscious residents General comparison; terms vary by operator. Check the offer and the contract. Prepaid is the right answer on your first day. You buy a card in a shop, at a kiosk or online, activate it, top it up with credit and choose a data package. There is no monthly commitment and nothing to cancel. The drawback is that prepaid rates for calls and data are often higher than the best contract prices, and credit or data packages can expire. A contract ( smlouva ) suits someone who will stay. You get a monthly allowance and sometimes a subsidised phone. The operator will want identification, and for foreigners may ask for a Czech address or for a residence document, depending on the operator's rules. Some operators may ask for a deposit or restrict the offer if your permit is for a short period. If you already hold a Czech bank account, direct debit is easy to arrange. A virtual operator sits between the two: a contract-like monthly plan, sometimes with no long commitment, delivered online. It can be the cheapest route for a resident who needs mostly data, but it is worth confirming which network it uses. What to compare Look at the price after the promotional period, not before. Many offers show a low price for the first months and a higher one afterwards. Read the line that says what the monthly fee becomes. Look at the data allowance, and at what happens when it runs out. Some plans slow the connection to a low speed; others block access until you buy more. "Unlimited" in a Czech advert often has a fair-use or speed condition, so find the sentence that qualifies it. Look at what is included in the EU. Under EU rules, calls and data used in other EU and EEA countries are charged as if you were at home, up to a fair-use limit, so a Czech plan works in most of Europe. Countries outside the EU, including the United Kingdom, can be charged differently, so check the operator's roaming page before you travel. Look at the commitment. A Czech consumer contract with a fixed term can run for up to 24 months under the Electronic Communications Act (as of 2026; check the official source). The cost of leaving early is set out in the contract. A phone on instalments, bought along with the plan, is a separate obligation from the service itself. Getting a number: a short guide Getting your first Czech number Start with prepaid if you are new Buy a prepaid SIM at a shop or an operator's store and take your passport or residence document. Activate and top up Follow the instructions on the card, or use the operator's app. Choose a data package. Test coverage where you live Use it for a few weeks at home and at work before committing to a contract. Compare contract offers Check the post-promotion price, the data rules and the commitment length. Keep your number if you switch Ask the new operator to port it. Do not cancel the old SIM first. An eSIM, a digital SIM that you install on a compatible phone by scanning a code, is offered by the major operators and by some virtual ones. It removes the need to visit a shop. Check that your phone supports it and that it is free of any operator lock, since a phone locked to a foreign operator will not accept a Czech SIM or eSIM. Keeping your number A Czech mobile number has nine digits and begins with a digit that marks it as mobile, with the country code +420 in front. You can move your number to another operator through number portability ( přenositelnost čísla ). The process is started by the new operator, which handles the transfer, so do not cancel your existing contract before the port is agreed. If you do, you can lose the number. This matters because your phone number is a login for a lot of things. Banks send codes to it, the state's electronic services may send one-time passwords to it, and delivery firms text it. A number that lapses can lock you out. For the services that use it, see how to use Czech public services online and Czech digital identity . Port first, cancel second Start the number transfer with the new operator before you end the old contract. Cancelling first can mean losing the number. A hypothetical first month Consider a hypothetical newcomer who lands with a phone that is locked to a foreign operator. On day one they buy a prepaid SIM, find it will not work, and discover the lock. The fix is to ask the home operator to release the lock, which can take days and sometimes a fee, or to buy a cheap unlocked handset. The sensible habit is to check the lock before the trip, and to carry the old SIM for the codes your foreign bank still sends. By the end of week two, the same newcomer has a Czech address, a bank account and a clearer idea of data use. At that point a contract or a virtual operator plan can be compared with real usage figures, taken from the prepaid app, rather than guesses. That is the cheapest way to avoid paying for an allowance you never touch. Shops, apps and the small print Operators sell through their own stores, partner shops, kiosks, supermarkets and online. Staff in stores can set up a SIM on the spot, and the larger stores in Prague often have English-speaking staff, though this varies by location and time of day. Kiosks and supermarkets sell prepaid cards but cannot advise on contracts. Whatever the channel, ask for the price list and the terms in writing, and ask when the introductory price ends. If you sign electronically, download a copy of the contract. A contract signed on a tablet at a counter is as binding as a paper one. Invoices, fees and problems Contract bills usually arrive electronically. Check that the first invoice matches the offer, and look for activation fees, device instalments and any add-on services such as insurance or premium content. If a fee appears that you did not agree to, ask the operator to remove it in writing. If you cannot resolve a dispute with the operator, complain to it in writing and keep the reply. For certain unresolved disputes about billing and services, the Czech Telecommunication Office offers a procedure. The Czech Trade Inspection Authority (ČOI) and other bodies handle other consumer complaints. The emergency number in Czechia and across the EU is 112, and it works without credit and even without a SIM card on most networks. Keep that in mind if you land with a locked phone. Frequently asked questions Can I use my foreign SIM in Czechia? Within the EU, roaming charges are limited, but it is rarely the cheapest way to live here. For anything beyond a short stay, a Czech number is easier for banks and delivery services. Do I need a Czech address for a contract? Often yes, or at least a residence document. Policies differ by operator, so ask before you queue. How long can a contract commitment be? For consumers the law limits the first commitment to 24 months (as of 2026; check the official source). Can I keep my number when I switch? Yes. Number portability lets you move it. The new operator starts the process. Buy a prepaid SIM on your first day, give the network a month in your actual flat, and only then compare contracts. Anything that depends on a Czech number, from bank codes to a data box login, is a reason to keep it live.
